newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seeks U.S. leniency in Cuba embargo arrests.
newsitem.headline: Spain seeks U.S. leniency in Cuba embargo arrests.

text.p: Spain asked the United States on Wednesday for leniency and a quick resolution in a U.S. court case that charges two Spanish businessmen with violating an American embargo on Cuba.
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes made the appeal in a meeting with U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs Jeffrey Davidow in Madrid.

"We presume they are innocent but we realise we cannot ask for a pardon," chief Spanish Foreign Ministry spokesman Inocencio Arias told Reuters. "We would like the public prosecution to be quick and lenient."

The two Spaniards, Javier Ferreiro-Parga and Juan Torres, were arrested in Miami on charges of breaking the embargo, trading with an enemy and money laundering. They allegedly shipped $350,000 worth of canned food, diapers and sanitary napkins from Miami to Cuba via the Dominican Republic.
Ferreiro was in a federal detention centre in Miami while Torres was free on bail there, both awaiting trial.
Davidow responded to Matutes' request by saying the U.S. judiciary was independent. Arias said Spain respected that independence.

"We don't like this law but we understand it's an internal matter," he said of the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba imposed in 1963. "We are not happy with a law that punishes trade during peacetime," Arias added.

Matutes also raised the matter of the two businessmen with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright when he accompanied Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on a state visit to Washington at the end of April.
Spain's year-old centre-right government has taken a harder line against Cuba than its Socialist predecessor, demanding all aid be linked to democratic reforms.
The policy shift, which has prompted several diplomatic incidents with Havana, has pleased Washington.
But Davidow acknowledged that the United States and Spain still disagreed on a number of questions regarding Latin America where Spain maintains a historical interest and influence.
Matutes reiterated Spain's opposition to the U.S. Helms-Burton law which seeks to penalise foreign companies trading with Cuba.
"We are against Helms-Burton. We don't have to go over it again," Arias said. "In policy toward Cuba, we have the same goals but the means are different."
Arias said there was no indication in the meeting that Washington was softening its stance toward Fidel Castro's regime.

The U.S. Congress passed the Helms-Burton law in 1996. It included provisions to punish third-country firms investing in property expropriated from U.S. citizens or firms after Castro's 1959 revolution.
The European Union had threatened to challenge the law in the World Trade Organisation.
But the crisis was defused last month when the EU agreed to set aside its challenge in return for a promise from Washington to establish a common policy on seized property.
The United States agreed to continue waiving a provision of the law that allows U.S. citizens to sue investors who profit from seized property.
Washington also said it would seek a change in another provision that bars executives of companies from investing in confiscated property from entering the United States.
But both U.S. and Spanish officials said the problems over Helms Burton have yet to be resolved satisfactorily.
